title: Model Selection Intelligence — The Right AI for Every Job

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By mid-2026, there are over 30 capable AI models available. Using the wrong model for a task costs money, time, or quality — sometimes all three. This lesson gives you a decision framework for choosing the right model for every situation: when to use Claude vs ChatGPT vs Gemini, when to use a small fast model vs a large capable one, and how to think about cost vs quality tradeoffs.

**The core principle:** No single model is best at everything. The most effective AI users in 2026 use 2-4 models, each doing what it's best at. Learning to route tasks to the right model is as important as learning to prompt.

## The Model Landscape (Mid-2026)

The four model families you need to understand:

**Anthropic Claude family:**
- **Claude Haiku 4.5** — Fastest, cheapest. Best for: classification, routing, yes/no decisions, short extraction, high-volume tasks where cost matters. Input: ~$1.00/M tokens.
- **Claude Sonnet 4.6** — Best value flagship. Best for: coding (79.6% SWE-bench Verified — industry leader), writing, analysis, most professional tasks. 1M token context in beta. Input: ~$3/M tokens.
- **Claude Opus 4.8** — Sustained complex autonomous work. Best for: long-horizon agentic coding, multi-step research, architectural decisions. Supports `xhigh` reasoning effort and 1M context. Input: ~$5/M tokens.
- **Claude Fable 5** — Most powerful Claude model. Adaptive thinking always on — reasons automatically on every request. State-of-the-art on FrontierCode and frontier physics/finance benchmarks. Input: $10/M tokens, Output: $50/M tokens. Use for hardest problems only.

**OpenAI GPT family:**
- **GPT-5.5** — Current OpenAI flagship. Fast, multimodal, broad ecosystem. Best for: image understanding, voice interaction (Advanced Voice Mode), data analysis (Code Interpreter), DALL-E image generation, connecting to third-party integrations. Input: $5/M tokens.
- **GPT-5.4** — Lower-cost frontier option. Input: $2.50/M. GPT-5.4 Mini ($0.75/M) and Nano ($0.20/M) for budget/high-volume tasks.
- **GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna** — Limited preview as of June 2026. Sol matches GPT-5.5 at same pricing; Terra matches GPT-5.4; Luna is a new budget tier.
- **o3** — OpenAI's primary 2026 reasoning model. Best for: complex multi-step reasoning, math, structured problem-solving. Input: $2/M, replaced o1 at 87% lower cost.
- **o4-mini** — Budget reasoning. Strong on STEM tasks at lower cost than o3.

**Google Gemini family:**
- **Gemini 2.5 Pro** — Largest context window (1M tokens), live web search, Deep Think reasoning mode. Best for: processing entire books or massive documents, real-time factual research, audio/video/image analysis, Google Workspace users.
- **Gemini 2.5 Flash** — Extremely fast, includes thinking capabilities. Best for: high-volume tasks, cost-sensitive production. ~$0.075-$0.30/M depending on thinking budget.
- **Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite** — Most cost-efficient Gemini. 1.5× faster than 2.0 Flash at lower cost. Best for: classification, translation, routing, high-scale summarisation.

**Open/local models:**
- **Llama 4 (Meta)** — Runs locally (via Ollama). Best for: privacy-sensitive tasks, offline use, no-cost experimentation at scale.
- **DeepSeek V4** — Open-weight, 1M context, thinking mode. Exceptional coding performance. API: ~$0.50/M input. Self-hostable.
- **Mistral Large** — Good value for writing tasks, European data residency option.
- **Qwen 2.5** — Strong multilingual capability, runs locally.

## The Task-to-Model Routing Guide

Use this as your reference when choosing a model:

**Writing & long-form content:**
→ **Claude Sonnet 4.6** — Best instruction-following, best writing quality, best at following complex style guides. Use Opus for final polish on high-stakes work.

**Coding & software engineering:**
→ **Claude Sonnet 4.6** for most coding tasks — 79.6% SWE-Bench Verified, best at autonomous code editing, debugging, and multi-file changes. **Claude Opus 4.8** for architectural decisions and complex systems.

**Research with current web information:**
→ **Perplexity AI** (built on Claude Opus) or **Gemini 2.5 Pro** — both have live web search. For one-off research: Perplexity. For integrated workflows: Gemini.

**Analysing large documents (50+ pages):**
→ **Gemini 2.5 Pro** (1M token context) for entire books, contracts, or codebases. **Claude** (200K context) for most normal-sized documents.

**Image, audio, or video analysis:**
→ **GPT-5.5** for image understanding and DALL-E generation. **Gemini 2.5 Pro** for audio/video (native multimodal) and **Gemini 2.5 Flash Image** for image editing. Claude handles images but is weaker than dedicated multimodal models.

**Third-party integrations (Zapier, Make, plugins):**
→ **ChatGPT / GPT-5.5** — largest third-party ecosystem. More tools connect to OpenAI than any other provider.

**Google Workspace users (Gmail, Docs, Sheets):**
→ **Gemini** — native integration into Google apps. Can read and write to your actual documents.

**Privacy-sensitive content:**
→ **Local models via Ollama** (Llama 4, Qwen 2.5, Mistral) — nothing leaves your machine. Or use **Claude** (Anthropic's privacy policy is strong for paid tier).

**High-volume, cost-sensitive tasks:**
→ **Gemini Flash** ($0.075/M input) or **GPT-4.1 Mini** ($0.15/M) or **Claude Haiku** ($1.00/M). At 1M+ tokens per day, model choice saves hundreds of dollars.

**Complex multi-step reasoning:**
→ **Claude Fable 5** (highest tier, adaptive thinking always on) or **Claude Opus 4.8 Extended Thinking** for long-horizon agentic tasks. **o3** (OpenAI) for structured math and problem-solving. **DeepSeek R1** for transparent/visible reasoning at lowest cost.

## The Multi-Model Strategy

The smartest AI users in 2026 don't pick one model — they route tasks:

**The $20/month optimal stack:**
- **Claude Pro ($20/month)** — All your writing, coding, analysis, and complex reasoning
- **Gemini free tier** — Google Workspace integration, large documents, real-time research
- **ChatGPT free tier** — Image analysis when needed, accessing GPT Store tools
- **Perplexity free tier** — Quick cited web research

This covers ~95% of professional use cases for $20/month.

**The power user stack:**
- Claude Pro + Perplexity Pro ($20 each)
- Gemini Advanced ($20/month) if you're in Google Workspace
- Ollama free (for local/privacy tasks)

**The production API stack** (if you're building tools or automations):
- Route to Claude Haiku or Gemini Flash for classification/routing steps (cheap)
- Route to Claude Sonnet for generation tasks (best value)
- Reserve Claude Opus for final review or complex decisions (expensive but worth it)
- Use caching for repeated system prompts (saves 50-90% on repeated calls)

## Understanding Cost — What Are You Actually Paying For?

AI models charge by **tokens** — roughly 4 characters = 1 token, or 750 words ≈ 1,000 tokens.

Typical task token counts:
- Simple classification or yes/no: 50-200 tokens
- Short email or paragraph: 300-500 tokens
- Full document analysis (5-page doc): 3,000-5,000 tokens
- Long-form report generation: 5,000-15,000 tokens
- Code generation for a feature: 2,000-8,000 tokens

**Cost comparison for 10,000 document analysis tasks (4,000 tokens each):**
- Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite: 40M tokens × $0.075 = **$3**
- GPT-5.4 Nano: 40M tokens × $0.20 = **$8**
- DeepSeek V4-Flash: 40M tokens × $0.50 = **$20**
- Claude Haiku 4.5: 40M tokens × $1.00 = **$40**
- Claude Sonnet 4.6: 40M tokens × $3.00 = **$120**
- GPT-5.5: 40M tokens × $5.00 = **$200**
- Claude Opus 4.8: 40M tokens × $5.00 = **$200**
- Claude Fable 5: 40M tokens × $10.00 = **$400**

For production automation: the difference between Flash-Lite and Fable 5 is ~130×. Route simple extraction tasks to cheap models; reserve premium models for decisions that require the highest quality.

**Prompt caching:** If you have a long system prompt you use repeatedly, Anthropic's prompt caching reduces the cost of re-sending it by up to 90%. For a 10,000-token system prompt sent 10,000 times, that's the difference between paying $3,000 and paying $300.

## Evaluating Model Output Quality

How do you know which model is actually better *for your specific task*? Run your own benchmark:

**The 5-task personal benchmark:**
1. Pick 5 representative tasks from your actual work
2. Send the same prompt (with the same context) to 2-3 models
3. Rate each output 1-5 on: accuracy, completeness, format, and tone
4. Note which model wins for each task type

This takes 30-45 minutes but gives you personal routing data that's more relevant than any published benchmark — because it tests *your* tasks, not standardised academic ones.

**Key quality signals to compare:**
- **Instruction following:** Did it do exactly what you asked, or did it add/remove things you didn't request?
- **Factual accuracy:** Can you verify the claims it made?
- **Format adherence:** If you asked for bullet points and got paragraphs, that's a fail
- **Appropriate length:** Did it pad or cut too much?
- **Tone:** Does it sound right for the context?

sections.title: Build Your Personal Model Routing Card
sections.content:
This workshop produces a personalised routing card — your reference for which model to use for each type of task you do regularly.

**Step 1 — List your top 8 AI tasks (5 minutes)**

Write down the 8 types of tasks you use AI for most often. Be specific:
- Not "writing" → "drafting client proposal emails"
- Not "research" → "researching competitor features for a product brief"
- Not "coding" → "debugging Python data pipeline scripts"

**Step 2 — Assign a draft model (5 minutes)**

Using the routing guide above, assign your best-guess model to each task.

**Step 3 — Run a 2-model comparison on your most important task (15 minutes)**

Pick your single most important task from the list. Send the same prompt to:
- **Claude** (claude.ai)
- **ChatGPT** (chatgpt.com) or **Gemini** (gemini.google.com)

Use real content — actual work content that represents what you normally do. Rate both outputs on: accuracy, completeness, format, tone (1-5 each).

**Step 4 — Create your routing card (10 minutes)**

Create a simple document with this format:

```
MY AI MODEL ROUTING CARD
Last updated: [date]

Task Type            | Primary Model | Fallback
---------------------|---------------|----------
[task 1]             | Claude Sonnet | Auto
[task 2]             | Gemini 2.5    | Claude
[task 3]             | Perplexity    | Claude
...

Notes:
- For large docs (>50 pages): always Gemini first
- For privacy-sensitive: local Llama via Ollama
- For Google Docs integration: Gemini
```

Save this somewhere accessible (Notion, desktop note). Update it when you discover a model is significantly better or worse than you expected.

sections.question: You need to analyse a 200-page industry report and extract all regulatory requirements mentioned, then cross-reference them with your company's current policies. Which model combination is best?
options: Claude Opus for the entire task — it's the most capable model
Use Gemini 2.5 Pro to analyse the full 200-page report (1M context handles it), then Claude to compare extracted requirements against your policy documents
Break the report into 20-page chunks and send to GPT-4.1 Mini for cost savings
Use Perplexity to research the regulatory requirements separately
sections.explanation: This is a perfect multi-model routing task. Gemini 2.5 Pro's 1M token context window can hold the full 200-page document (roughly 150,000 words = ~200,000 tokens) in a single context, making it ideal for the extraction step. Claude is then ideal for the comparison and synthesis step because of its superior instruction-following and analytical writing. Claude Opus alone (A) can't hold a 200-page document in one go (200K token limit). Chunking (C) loses cross-document context. Perplexity (D) researches the web, not your specific document.

sections.title: Workshop A — Model Capability Mapping
sections.content:
Map the capability differences between available AI models.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** "Compare Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus on these dimensions: reasoning depth, code generation quality, creative writing, following complex instructions, knowledge breadth, and speed. For each model, describe its sweet spot."

**Step 2 — Test the same prompt** on Haiku and Sonnet:
Prompt: "Design a system architecture for a real-time multiplayer game with 10,000 concurrent players. Include: technology stack, data flow, scaling strategy, and the 3 most important trade-offs."

**Step 3 — Compare the responses.** Where does quality differ? Is the quality difference worth the cost difference for your use case?

**Step 4 — Build a personal model selection matrix** for your most common tasks.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build an Intelligent Model Router
sections.content:
Implement a model router that selects the right AI for each task.

**Step 1 — Define your routing criteria:**
- Task complexity (simple → Haiku, complex → Sonnet)
- Privacy requirements (sensitive → local model)
- Speed requirement (real-time → Haiku, async → Sonnet)
- Cost budget (high volume → Haiku, important decisions → Sonnet)

**Step 2 — Ask Claude Code** to implement the router:
```
Build a model_router function that:
1. Takes a task description and metadata (privacy_level, response_time, importance, budget_tier)
2. Applies routing rules to select the optimal model
3. Logs the routing decision and reasoning
4. Falls back to Haiku if routing is uncertain
5. Includes a cost estimator for the selected model
```

**Step 3 — Test with 10 diverse task descriptions.** Are the routing decisions correct?

**Step 4 — Mandatory review:** Ask Claude: *"Review the routing logic. What task types will be systematically misrouted?"*

sections.title: Workshop C — Task-Specific Model Benchmarking
sections.content:
Benchmark models on YOUR specific tasks, not generic benchmarks.

**Step 1 — Create 5 test prompts** representative of your actual work.

**Step 2 — Run each prompt** on both Haiku and Sonnet.

**Step 3 — Evaluate each response** on: accuracy, completeness, usefulness for your specific context.

**Step 4 — Calculate:** For each task type, what is the quality difference (0-100%) and the cost difference?

**Step 5 — Find your "good enough threshold":** For which tasks is Haiku within 10% of Sonnet quality? Those tasks should use Haiku in production.

sections.title: Workshop D — Dynamic Model Selection in Your Application
sections.content:
Add dynamic model selection to your AI application.

**Step 1 — Take an existing AI feature** in your project or one from earlier in this course.

**Step 2 — Implement a A/B testing framework:**
```
Add A/B testing that:
- Routes 20% of requests to Sonnet, 80% to Haiku
- Measures output quality via user feedback or automated metrics
- Tracks cost per request for each model
- Generates a weekly report: quality vs cost for each model
```

**Step 3 — Run the A/B test** for at least 50 requests.

**Step 4 — Analyse results:** Is Sonnet significantly better for this specific task? Is the cost premium justified?

**Step 5 — Make a data-driven model selection decision** for this feature.

sections.question: You're building a customer service bot that handles both simple FAQs and complex technical support. The most cost-efficient architecture is:
options: Use only Haiku for all requests to minimise cost
Use only Sonnet for all requests to maximise quality
Route simple FAQ requests to Haiku and complex technical issues to Sonnet based on intent classification
Randomly assign 50% to each model and average the results
sections.explanation: Tiered routing gives you cost efficiency where it's safe (FAQs have predictable, verifiable answers) and quality where it matters (complex technical support where wrong answers damage trust). Implementation: first classify the request type using a small, fast model or rule-based classifier; then route accordingly. Monitor: track when Haiku-handled requests escalate to human support (suggests misrouting or quality gap).

sections.question: A new AI model is released claiming "10× better performance" on benchmarks. Should you immediately switch your production application to it?
options: No — evaluate it on your specific tasks first. General benchmarks often don't reflect task-specific performance, and "better" on a benchmark may not mean better for your use case
Yes if it's from a reputable provider
No — always wait 6 months for new models to stabilise
sections.explanation: Benchmark performance rarely translates directly to task-specific performance. Evaluate any new model by: (1) running your specific test prompts and comparing outputs, (2) checking whether the new model behaves differently on edge cases your application encounters, (3) testing performance and latency, (4) verifying cost. Only switch after you can confirm the new model outperforms the current one on your actual tasks, not just on published benchmarks.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 18-2.** You now have a routing framework for every major AI model, a cost comparison for scale decisions, and a personal routing card methodology. The right model for the right task is one of the highest-leverage skills in professional AI use.
